extracted.intended_audience: students, theorists, and reformers of public administration and representative government; legislators and civic architects
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for allocating functions between local and central authorities and for constituting and supervising local representative and executive bodies. Covers what duties are local or national, how to organize representation and appointment, and how central supervision should operate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinct roles of execution and control
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of the elective body is not to do the work, but to see that it is properly done, and that nothing necessary is left undone; subdivision useful for execution does not apply to control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single superintending body can supervise multiple departments better than minute microscopic control. It is absurd that every workman should be looked after by a superintendent to himself; control should be collective and comprehensive rather than extremely subdivided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elective body as supervisory, not executive
rubrics_metrics.description: An elective local council's proper business is to consider the interest of the locality as a whole, composed of parts which must be adapted to one another, and attended to in the order and ratio of their importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local councils should exercise oversight and coordinate local concerns rather than perform technical functions themselves; examples include adapting parts of local administration to one another and prioritizing by importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of superior minds in local bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Every local body should contain a portion of the very best minds of the locality, brought into perpetual contact with minds of a lower grade to raise political intelligence and ensure enlightened and honest performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local institutions function as schools of political capacity; without presence of higher-order characters and due surveillance, bodies often degenerate into pursuit of members' self-interest. Small piecemeal offices seldom attract high-quality persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for municipal representation (village exclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere village has no claim to a municipal representation; places whose inhabitants are not markedly distinguished from surrounding rural districts should be merged into larger circumscriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small places rarely have a sufficient public to furnish a tolerable municipal council; talent is often concentrated in one man who dominates. Merge into larger units to avoid domination and ensure workable councils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation areas should match kinds of local business
rubrics_metrics.description: Different kinds of local business require different areas of representation; geographical considerations and community of interest determine appropriate constituencies (e.g., unions of parishes for relief of indigence; county-scale for highways, prisons, police).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an organizational basis suited to the functional requirements: e.g., Unions of parishes for poor-relief; average county area may suffice for police and prisons. Modify the maxim that a local elective body should have authority over all local concerns when function-specific scale differs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve higher-description business for larger boards when higher qualifications needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Where higher qualifications are obtainable for a County Board than for smaller bodies, it may be expedient to reserve some higher descriptions of local business to the County Board rather than each separate Union managing them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specialized or important duties would be better handled by more qualified persons available at a larger scale, allocate those duties upward to secure competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single executive officer, singly responsible
rubrics_metrics.description: Each executive officer should be single, and singly responsible for the whole of the duty committed to his charge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plural executive offices for the same duty; single responsibility clarifies accountability and reduces shirking/fragmentation of blame.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive appointments should be by nomination, not popular election
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive officers (e.g., surveyor, health officer, collector of rates) should be nominated, not elected, because popular choice usually depends on local interest or sympathy and is often a farce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointments by the local representative body are also objectionable because such bodies tend to become joint-stock associations for carrying out private jobs. Prefer appointment on individual responsibility of the chairman or analogous local executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized appointment responsibility (chairman/mayor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments should be made on the individual responsibility of the chairman of the body (mayor or equivalent); he occupies a local position analogous to the prime minister and should be charged with appointment and watching of local officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chairman should be appointed by the council from its own number, subject to annual re-election or removal by vote of the body. This concentrates responsibility and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: All purely local business devolves to local authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: All business purely local--all which concerns only a single locality--should devolve upon the local authorities (e.g., paving, lighting, cleansing of streets, house drainage in ordinary circumstances).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nation is concerned only insofar as it is interested in the private well-being of citizens; local authorities should handle matters confined to the locality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify national-interest local functions requiring central regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some functions performed by local bodies are really national because the whole nation is interested in their administration (e.g., jails, local police, local administration of justice) and should be uniformly regulated and under central superintendence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad local management in these areas can harm the whole country; central laws and enforcement should ensure uniform standards (security of person and property, equal justice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Central appointment of inspectors for locally-managed national duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where localities administer duties imposed by central authority, the central government should appoint inspectors to see that local officers do their duty (examples: inspectors of prisons, factories, schools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inspectors ensure compliance with parliamentary rules and can suggest new rules where needed; central oversight mitigates local ignorance or neglect of national standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central supremacy on principles; local competence in details
rubrics_metrics.description: The authority most conversant with principles should be supreme over principles, while that most competent in details should have the details left to it; the principal business of the central authority is to give instruction, and of the local authority to apply it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Power may be localized but knowledge centralized: central organs (minister or functionary) should collect and disseminate experience, advise, and ensure uniform principles are applied locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central role: perpetual communication, advice, publicity, and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: The central authority ought to keep open perpetual communication with localities—informing itself by their experience, them by its own; giving advice freely and volunteering it when necessary; compelling publicity and recordation of proceedings; and enforcing obedience to general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central government acts as teacher, critic, and enforcer—compelling recordation, public scrutiny, and obedience to laws to prevent local mismanagement that prejudices others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislature should prescribe modes of taxation and principles of relief
rubrics_metrics.description: While leaving the mere amount of local taxes to local discretion, the Legislature should lay down authoritatively the mode of taxation and rules of assessment permitted and prescribe the principles for awarding public charity (poor relief).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prevents local bodies from imposing unjust burdens on particular classes and ensures national standards for relief that affect industry and morality of laboring population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible central interference and extraordinary remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Central power may be required in extreme cases to dissolve a local representative council or dismiss the local executive, but not to make new appointments or suspend local institutions; laws should define penalties and enforcement modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central interference should be limited and defined by law; executive branches should act as adviser, critic, and denouncer to Parliament or local constituencies when local conduct is condemnable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local institutions as educational, requiring supervisory teachers
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular local institutions are instruments of political education; the education is poor if it associates ignorance with ignorance—what is wanted is to make ignorance aware of itself via contact with superior minds and proper supervision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not eliminate the teacher: local bodies need higher-order characters (teachers/supervisors) to make political schooling effective; purely leaving people to manage without guidance leads to bad instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Territorial organization should respect nationality where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally necessary for free institutions that government boundaries coincide mainly with those of nationalities, because free institutions are next to impossible in countries made up of different nationalities lacking common sympathies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National feeling (language, religion, political antecedents) supports the united public opinion necessary for representative government. Geographical intermixture or absorption may complicate or mitigate this principle; practical exceptions exist where intermixture makes separation impracticable.
